edges.effect_quant: Early-life antibiotic exposure was associated with higher childhood asthma risk in a 2025 cohort of 1,091,449 children (HR 1.24) and in a pooled analysis of four cohorts in 2017 (OR 2.18), but sibling-adjusted nationwide data suggest part of the relationship reflects confounding by infections and family factors.
edges.population: children exposed to antibiotics during fetal life, infancy, or the first years of life
edges.mechanism: Antibiotics early in life may alter airway-relevant immune maturation indirectly through microbiome disruption, especially during the period when microbial exposures shape Th1/Th2 balance and mucosal tolerance. At the same time, respiratory infections that prompt antibiotics can mimic a causal signal, which is why the most rigorous studies still point to a likely smaller effect than crude associations suggest.
edges.summary: Early-life antibiotics appear associated with higher asthma risk, but this edge is more confounded and controversial than the IBD signal. Large cohorts still show a positive association, especially with repeated antibiotic courses, yet sibling and infection-adjusted analyses indicate that some of the apparent effect is explained by familial or indication-related factors rather than pure antibiotic causality.
edges.caveats: This is not a simple causal story: children who receive early antibiotics are also more likely to have infections or family contexts that raise asthma risk on their own. The fairest reading is a modest harmful association with substantial residual confounding, not a headline-grabbing proof that antibiotics directly cause asthma.

evidence.notes: Antibiotics in fetal and early life and subsequent childhood asthma: nationwide population based study with sibling analysis.

evidence.citation: Beier MA et al 2025 J Infect Dis
evidence.notes: Early Childhood Antibiotics and Chronic Pediatric Conditions: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
